summary: The RSVP ASSOCIATION object links recovery label switched paths to the paths they protect in GMPLS. This informational RFC reviews how association is used in GMPLS recovery and defines no new procedures.

plainLanguage.summary: It links a spare route to the main route, like writing on a spare tire which car it belongs to.

questions: what is the rsvp association object
how does gmpls recovery use association
what is end-to-end recovery in gmpls
how are working and backup lsps linked
subtitle: How backup routes are linked to the paths they protect in optical networks.

tldr.problem: In optical networks (GMPLS), when a backup path is set up to protect a working path, there needs to be a way to record which backup protects which working path so network elements can manage them together.
tldr.mechanism: The RSVP ASSOCIATION object is used to tag both the working path and the backup path with matching information that identifies them as protecting and protected paths. The match is made using an Association Type field (set to 'Recovery'), an Association Source address, and an Association ID.
tldr.outcome: Network elements can immediately identify which paths are related, coordinate their protection, and manage fast rerouting without confusion.

facts.label: Association ID field
facts.value: LSP ID of working or recovery path

today: RFC 6689 is an Informational RFC that clarifies the use of existing recovery mechanisms in GMPLS. It is still authoritative for implementations of GMPLS fast reroute and protection switching in optical and multi-layer networks.

sections.title: Linking Paths in GMPLS Recovery
sections.content:
In a GMPLS network, an Label Switched Path (LSP) is a tunnel through the network. A working LSP carries the customer's real traffic. A recovery LSP (also called a protection or backup LSP) is a separate path that is pre-established to take over instantly if the working path fails.

The problem is: how do network elements know which recovery LSP belongs with which working LSP? Both are just RSVP messages that look similar on the surface. The solution is the ASSOCIATION object, which is carried in the RSVP Path message for both the working LSP and the recovery LSP. By carrying matching ASSOCIATION objects, the two LSPs can be correlated and linked.

This document does not define any new mechanisms or procedures for GMPLS recovery. It simply clarifies and documents how the ASSOCIATION object is to be used in the recovery context, as defined in RFC 4872 and RFC 4873. It answers questions that implementers have repeatedly asked about the proper interpretation of the object.
sections.plainLanguage: A working route and a backup route are both RSVP paths. They need to say "we are a pair" so routers know to switch from the working path to the backup when the working path breaks.

sections.title: The ASSOCIATION Object
sections.content:
An ASSOCIATION object is carried in RSVP Path messages and has four important fields. The Association Type field identifies what kind of association this is. For recovery, the type is set to "Recovery". The Association Source is an IP address associated with the node that created the association, usually the tunnel sender address of the working LSP. The Association ID is a numeric identifier that further identifies which specific paths are associated.

An LSP can carry multiple ASSOCIATION objects at the same time. For example, it might carry one ASSOCIATION object for recovery (linking it to a backup), a second one for segment recovery (linking it to a separate segment-level backup), and a third for resource sharing (linking it to other LSPs that share resources). Downstream nodes compare all fields of the ASSOCIATION object to determine which LSPs are linked.

The Association ID can take several forms. It might be set to the LSP ID of the working path (if the working path is already signaled and known), the LSP ID of the recovery path (if the recovery path is signaled first), or, if neither is yet known, the LSP's own LSP ID as a default.
sections.plainLanguage: An ASSOCIATION object is like a label that says "this path is a backup for the path with ID X". Both the working and backup paths carry labels that mention each other.

sections.title: End-to-End Recovery Associations
sections.content:
In end-to-end recovery, a working LSP and recovery LSP have the same source and destination, but follow different routes. Both use ASSOCIATION objects with the same Association Type (Recovery) and the same Association Source (the tunnel sender address of the working LSP).

The Association ID field in both paths will match, but the RFC allows for three different cases depending on the order in which the paths are signaled.

Case 1: The working LSP is signaled first and carries an ASSOCIATION object with the Association ID set to its own LSP ID. When the recovery LSP is signaled later, it carries the same ASSOCIATION object, and the downstream node sees that both carry the same Association ID and concludes they are a pair.

Case 2: The recovery LSP is signaled first (used in shared 1:N protection where one backup protects multiple working paths). It carries an ASSOCIATION object with its own LSP ID. Each working LSP, when signaled, carries the same ASSOCIATION object and they are matched by Association ID.

Case 3: Both paths are signaled concurrently. The working LSP carries an ASSOCIATION object with the Association ID set to the recovery LSP's ID, and the recovery LSP carries one with the working LSP's ID. When they meet at a downstream node, the node performs bidirectional matching to associate them.
sections.plainLanguage: The working path says "I am protected by path 42". The backup says "I protect path 99". When they meet, a router can match them up.

sections.title: Segment Recovery Associations
sections.content:
Segment recovery protects just one segment of a longer path, not the entire end-to-end path. For example, a very long path that crosses three domains might be protected only in the middle domain.

Segment recovery uses the same ASSOCIATION object as end-to-end recovery (same Association Type of "Recovery"), but the Association Source is different: it is set to the tunnel sender address of the segment recovery LSP, not the working LSP's tunnel sender address. This makes it clear that the segment recovery is rooted elsewhere in the network.

Segment recovery uses Case 2 behavior only: the segment recovery LSP is signaled first with its own LSP ID, and each segment-level working LSP carries the same ASSOCIATION object and is matched by Association ID. Case 3 (concurrent signaling with bidirectional matching) does not apply to segment recovery because the endpoint addresses differ between the segment-level working and recovery LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: A segment backup works the same way as an end-to-end backup, but it protects only one segment of the path, not the whole thing.

sections.title: Changing Associations Over Time
sections.content:
The RFC allows that ASSOCIATION objects can be added to or changed on an LSP during its lifetime. For example, a working LSP might be signaled initially without any ASSOCIATION object, and then later when a recovery LSP is signaled, the working LSP is updated to carry the appropriate ASSOCIATION object to link them.

Similarly, the Association ID value in an ASSOCIATION object can change during the lifetime of an LSP. However, the RFC does not define when or how such changes should happen. Care must be taken when changing the Association ID to ensure that the old association is not lost during the transition. The RFC does not require that Association IDs be changed (it uses the word "MAY"), and in fact, most implementations are expected to use a static Association ID for the lifetime of an LSP.

When multiple ASSOCIATION objects are present on an LSP, they must all be examined to find all associations. If an LSP is updated and an ASSOCIATION object is removed, the downstream node must be aware that the association has been dissolved.
sections.plainLanguage: Paths can add or change their association labels over time, but it should be done carefully so the pair does not get separated by accident.
